Which is used for things, not people.
The commas indicate that this is additional information.
Why not the others?
that – usually used in restrictive clauses without commas ❌
who – used for people ❌
what – not used as a relative pronoun here ❌

questions.question: Nazrul, ----- is our national poet, was also a soldier.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The clause “who is our national poet” is a non-restrictive relative clause giving additional information about Nazrul.
Who is used for people when they are the subject of the relative clause.
Why not the others?
whom – used for objects, not subjects ❌
he – would start a new sentence, not a relative clause ❌
what – not used for people ❌

questions.question: The lady ----- I am sending this letter to is a friend of my cousin's.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The lady is the object of the verb phrase “am sending this letter to.”
Whom is used as the object relative pronoun in formal English.
Why not the others?
which – refers to things, not people ❌
whose – shows possession, not correct here ❌
who – used for subjects, but the lady is the object here ❌

questions.question: They developed a program ----- has been refined many times over the years.[]
questions.explanation:
Why others are wrong:
A. it ❌ → Would create two separate clauses (grammatically incorrect).
B. who ❌ → Used for people, not things.
D. those ❌ → Demonstrative pronoun, not a relative pronoun.

questions.question: I know the boy ----- is there.[]
questions.explanation:
Why others are wrong:
A. whom ❌ → Used as an object, not as a subject.
C. which ❌ → Used for things, not people.
D. that one ❌ → Not a correct relative pronoun in this structure.

questions.question: He was reading a book, the name of ----- I have forgotten.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is: “He was reading a book, the name of ___ I have forgotten.”
Here, we need a relative pronoun after the preposition “of.”
When a preposition (like of) comes before the relative pronoun, we use:
which → for things
whom → for people
Since book is a thing, we use which.
✔ Correct sentence:  He was reading a book, the name of which I have forgotten.
Why others are wrong:
A. that ❌ → “That” is not used after a preposition.
B. whose ❌ → Used to show possession (e.g., the boy whose book…).
C. what ❌ → Not used as a relative pronoun after a noun like this.

questions.question: I haven't met Mr. Sattar, ----- painting you admire so much.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is: “I haven't met Mr. Sattar, ___ painting you admire so much.”
We need a relative pronoun showing possession.
The painting belongs to Mr. Sattar.
To show possession, we use whose (for both people and things).
✔ Correct sentence:  I haven't met Mr. Sattar, whose painting you admire so much.
Why others are wrong:
A. who ❌ → Used as subject, not for possession.
B. whom ❌ → Used as object, not for possession.
D. which ❌ → Used for things, not to show possession of a person.

questions.question: You met four people -------.[]
options: one of whom was my brother
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“You met four people ____.”
We need a relative clause to add information about the four people.
The idea is: Among the four people you met, one was my brother.
When referring to one out of a group, we use “one of whom”.
✔ Correct sentence:
 You met four people, one of whom was my brother.
Why others are wrong:
B. who was my brother ❌ → Implies all four people were your brother, which is wrong.
C. whose one was my brother ❌ → Grammatically incorrect.
D. whom my brother was ❌ → Nonsense structure, incorrect.

questions.question: They are two brothers, but ----- of them was honest.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“They are two brothers, but ___ of them was honest.”
We are talking about two brothers, and the sentence implies not one of them was honest.
neither → means not one of two, which fits perfectly here.
either → means one or the other (positive choice), so it’s wrong.
both → means the two together, which contradicts the sentence.
not one → could work grammatically, but neither is the correct, natural choice for two people.

questions.question: Each of them was present. Here, what type of pronoun 'each' is ---[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Each of them was present.”
Each refers to every individual in a group separately.
Pronouns that distribute or single out members of a group are called distributive pronouns.
Other types of pronouns:
Reflexive pronoun ❌ → Refers back to the subject (e.g., himself, herself).
Relative pronoun ❌ → Introduces a relative clause (e.g., who, which, that).
Emphatic pronoun ❌ → Emphasizes a noun (e.g., I myself, she herself).

questions.question: Which of the following sentence is correct ?[]
options: Any of the three pen will do
Any of the three pens will do
Either of the three pen will do
Either of the three pens will do
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is about choosing one from a group of three pens.
“Any” refers to one or more out of a group, and it must agree with the plural noun that follows “of the”.
Correct: pens (plural)
Wrong: pen (singular)
“Either” ❌ → Refers specifically to one of two, not three.
✔ Correct sentence:
 Any of the three pens will do.
Why others are wrong:
A. Any of the three pen ❌ → “pen” should be plural: pens.
C. Either of the three pen ❌ → “Either” is only for two items; also singular noun wrong.
D. Either of the three pens ❌ → “Either” cannot refer to three items.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.[]
options: A few of the three boys got a prize
Every of the three boys got a prize
All of the three boys got a prize
Each of the three boys got a prize
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is about three boys individually receiving a prize.
Each → emphasizes every individual separately, which fits here.
All → emphasizes the group collectively, not individuals.
Every ❌ → should be followed by “boy”, not “of the three boys”.
A few ❌ → implies some, not all three.
✔ Correct sentence:
 Each of the three boys got a prize.

questions.question: Each of the ladies told ----- own story.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Each of the ladies told ___ own story.”
Each is a distributive pronoun, referring to every individual separately.
Since ladies are female, the singular possessive pronoun matching each individual is “her.”
✔ Correct sentence:
 Each of the ladies told her own story.
Why others are wrong:
A. its ❌ → Used for things or animals, not people.
C. their ❌ → Plural possessive; “each” is singular.
D. hers ❌ → Independent possessive pronoun, not used before “own story.”

questions.question: Each of the workers has done ----- job.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Each of the workers has done ___ job.”
Each is a distributive pronoun, referring to every individual separately.
When referring to a singular person or thing, we use a singular possessive pronoun.
Traditionally, “his” is used as a generic singular pronoun in such cases.
✔ Correct sentence:
 Each of the workers has done his job.
Why others are wrong:
A. their ❌ → Plural possessive; “each” is singular.
B. her ❌ → Only for females, not generic.
C. whose ❌ → Relative pronoun, not a possessive in this context.

questions.question: Everyone of you should do ----- duty.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Everyone of you should do ___ duty.”
Everyone refers to all the people individually.
Since the sentence is directly addressing “you”, the possessive pronoun should match the person being spoken to.
The correct possessive here is “your.”
✔ Correct sentence:
 Everyone of you should do your duty.
Why others are wrong:
A. his ❌ → Would be used if referring to a singular male generically, not in direct address.
B. their ❌ → Usually works for plural, but with “everyone of you”, “your” is better and more natural.
D. one's ❌ → Formal generic, but not suitable in direct address.

questions.question: Neither of the two men wants ----- son educated.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Neither of the two men wants ___ son educated.”
Neither refers to not one of two, which is singular.
Therefore, the singular possessive pronoun is needed.
Since it refers to a man, the correct pronoun is “his.”
✔ Correct sentence:
Neither of the two men wants his son educated.
Why others are wrong:
A. their ❌ → Plural possessive; “neither” is singular.
C. them ❌ → Object pronoun, not possessive.
D. its ❌ → Refers to things or animals, not men.

questions.question: The pronoun is agreed with its antecedent in ---[]
options: Each of the companies had their books audited
Each of these companies had it's books audited
Each of these companies had its books audited
Each of these companies had their books audited
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Each of these companies had ___ books audited.”
Each is a distributive pronoun → singular, even though it refers to multiple companies.
The pronoun must agree in number with the singular “each”, not the plural “companies.”
The correct singular possessive pronoun is “its.”
✔ Correct sentence:
 Each of these companies had its books audited.
Why others are wrong:
A. Each of the companies had their books audited ❌ → “their” is plural; “each” is singular.
B. Each of these companies had it's books audited ❌ → “it’s” is a contraction of it is, not a possessive.
D. Each of these companies had their books audited ❌ → Again, “their” is plural; incorrect agreement.

questions.question: Either of the ----- to blame for the damage.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Either of the ___ to blame for the damage.”
Either refers to one of two, so the subject is singular.
Therefore, the verb must also be singular → is.
And since we are choosing one from two girls, we say “two girls” after “either of the…”
✔ Correct sentence:
 Either of the two girls is to blame for the damage.
Why others are wrong:
A. three girls ❌ → “Either” can only refer to two items, not three.
B. three girls have ❌ → Wrong number (three) and wrong verb form; “either” only works with two.
C. two girls are ❌ → Plural verb “are” does not match the singular “either.”

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.[]
options: Each of the men and women are bound to obey the law of the country
Each of the men and women is bound to obey the law of the country
Each of the men and women were bound to obey the law of the country
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Each of the men and women ___ bound to obey the law of the country.”
Each is a distributive pronoun → always singular, even if it refers to multiple people.
Therefore, the verb must also be singular → is.
✔ Correct sentence:
 Each of the men and women is bound to obey the law of the country.
Why others are wrong:
A. …are bound ❌ → “are” is plural; does not agree with singular “each.”
C. …were bound ❌ → “were” is past plural; “each” is singular, so wrong tense/number.
D. None of the above ❌ → B is correct, so this is wrong.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: Neither of the roads lead to the railway station
Neither of the roads leads to the railway station
Neither of the roads are leading to the railway station
Neither roads are led to the railway station
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Neither of the roads ___ to the railway station.”
Neither refers to not one of two, so it is singular.
The verb must therefore be singular → leads.
✔ Correct sentence:
 Neither of the roads leads to the railway station.
Why others are wrong:
A. …lead ❌ → “lead” is plural; does not agree with singular “neither.”
C. …are leading ❌ → Plural verb, also continuous tense is unnecessary here.
D. Neither roads are led ❌ → Incorrect structure; “neither” always takes singular, and “are led” is passive incorrectly used here.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: Neither of those mattresses feel comfortable
Neither of those mattresses are feeling comfortable
Neither of those mattresses feels comfortable
Neither of those mattresses have felt comfortable
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Neither of those mattresses ___ comfortable.”
Neither refers to not one of two, so it is singular.
The verb must agree with the singular subject → feels.
✔ Correct sentence:
 Neither of those mattresses feels comfortable.
Why others are wrong:
A. …feel ❌ → Plural verb; “neither” is singular.
B. …are feeling ❌ → Plural verb and continuous tense is unnecessary.
D. …have felt ❌ → Plural verb; “neither” is singular, and present perfect is not needed here.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: Neither of these two women are to be trusted
Neither of these two woman are to be trusted
Neither of these two women is  to be trusted
Neither of those two woman are to be trusted
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“Neither of these two women ___ to be trusted.”
Neither refers to not one of two, which is singular.
Therefore, the verb must be singular → is.
Women is the correct plural form of woman.
✔ Correct sentence:
 Neither of these two women is to be trusted.
Why others are wrong:
A. …are ❌ → Plural verb; “neither” is singular.
B. …woman are ❌ → “woman” should be plural (women) and verb should be singular.
D. …woman are ❌ → Same errors: singular noun and plural verb; also “those” instead of “these” is less precise if context is “these two women.”

questions.question: They two love 'each other'. It is an example of ---[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“They two love each other.”
“Each other” shows a mutual action between two people.
Pronouns that express mutual or reciprocal action are called reciprocal pronouns.
Other types of pronouns for comparison:
Personal pronoun ❌ → Refers to a specific person (e.g., I, you, he, she).
Relative pronoun ❌ → Introduces a relative clause (e.g., who, which, that).
Indefinite pronoun ❌ → Refers to an unspecified person or thing (e.g., someone, anyone, all).

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: The three sisters love each other
The three sisters love one another
The three sisters loves one another
The three sisters loved each other
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“They two love each other.”
“Each other” shows a mutual action between the two people.
Pronouns that express mutual or reciprocal action are called reciprocal pronouns.
Other options:
A. Personal pronoun ❌ → Refers to a specific person (e.g., I, you, he, she), but does not show mutual action.
B. Relative pronoun ❌ → Introduces a relative clause (e.g., who, which, that).
C. Indefinite pronoun ❌ → Refers to an unspecified person or thing (e.g., someone, anyone, all).

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence.[]
options: The family members love to each other
The family members love away each other
The family members love between each other
The family members love each other
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is about mutual love among three people:
“The three sisters ___.”
When talking about mutual actions among more than two people, the correct reciprocal pronoun is “one another”.
“Each other” is typically used for two people.
The verb must agree with the plural subject “three sisters” → love (not loves).
✔ Correct sentence:
The three sisters love one another.
Why others are wrong:
A. …love each other ❌ → “Each other” is generally for two people, not three.
C. …loves one another ❌ → Verb “loves” does not agree with plural subject.
D. …loved each other ❌ → Past tense is possible, but the standard answer is present tense, and “each other” is less correct for three people.

questions.question: The pronoun agrees with its antecedent in.[]
options: The family does their best to make a living
The family are doing its best to make a living
The family is doing their best to make a living
The family does its best to make a living
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“The family ___ best to make a living.”
Family is a collective noun.
When the family is considered as a single unit, it is singular, so the verb must be singular → does.
The possessive pronoun must also match the singular sense → its.
✔ Correct sentence:
 The family does its best to make a living.
Why others are wrong:
A. The family does their best ❌ → “their” is plural; mismatch with singular “family.”
B. The family are doing its best ❌ → “are” is plural; mismatch with singular “its.”
C. The family is doing their best ❌ → “their” is plural; singular subject needs “its.”

questions.question: Which one is the correct sentence ?[]
options: The jury is giving its verdict today
The jury are giving its verdict today
The juries is giving its verdict today
The juries are giving its verdict today
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“The jury ___ giving its verdict today.”
Jury is a collective noun.
When a collective noun is considered as a single unit, it takes a singular verb → is.
The possessive pronoun should also match the singular sense → its.
✔ Correct sentence:
 The jury is giving its verdict today.
Why others are wrong:
B. The jury are giving its verdict today ❌ → “are” is plural; does not match singular sense of “jury.”
C. The juries is giving its verdict today ❌ → “Juries” is plural; should use “are,” not “is.”
D. The juries are giving its verdict today ❌ → Plural subject “juries” does not match singular possessive “its.”

questions.question: An elephant ----- vigorously when it is overheated.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“An elephant ___ vigorously when it is overheated.”
Subject: An elephant (singular)
Verb: should agree with singular subject → flaps
Possessive pronoun: refers to its own ears → its
✔ Correct sentence:
 An elephant flaps its ears vigorously when it is overheated.
Why others are wrong:
A. flapping it ears ❌ → Wrong tense; “it” should be “its.”
B. it ears flap ❌ → Incorrect word order; subject-verb agreement wrong.
D. ears flap it ❌ → Completely wrong word order and grammar.

questions.question: I have got a week to finish this, ----- is just about long enough.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“I have got a week to finish this, ___ is just about long enough.”
The clause “is just about long enough” refers to the whole preceding noun phrase “a week to finish this.”
When a relative pronoun refers to a thing or a whole idea, we use “which.”
✔ Correct sentence:
I have got a week to finish this, which is just about long enough.
Why others are wrong:
A. what ❌ → Not used as a relative pronoun in this context.
C. that ❌ → Can introduce restrictive clauses, but after a comma referring to the whole idea, “which” is correct.
D. who ❌ → Refers to people, not things or ideas.

questions.question: Nila couldn't come to the party, ----- was a pity.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The clause “was a pity” refers to the whole preceding idea (that Nila couldn’t come).
When a relative pronoun refers to a whole idea or situation, we use “which.”
✔ Correct sentence:
 Nila couldn't come to the party, which was a pity.
Why others are wrong:
A. who ❌ → Refers to people, not a whole idea.
C. what ❌ → Not used as a relative pronoun here.
D. that ❌ → Can introduce a clause but not after a comma referring to the whole idea.

questions.question: ----- is a princess.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
“___ is a princess.”
The subject refers to a female person.
The personal pronoun for a singular female is “she.”
✔ Correct sentence:
She is a princess.
Why others are wrong:
A. He ❌ → Refers to a male.
C. We ❌ → Refers to a group including the speaker.
D. They ❌ → Refers to multiple people.

questions.question: নিচের কোনটি personal pronoun ?[]
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
Personal Pronoun এমন pronoun যা কোনো ব্যক্তি বা বস্তুর পরিবর্তে সরাসরি ব্যবহৃত হয়।
 উদাহরণ:
I, You, He, She, It, We, They
এখানে —
Any → Indefinite pronoun
This → Demonstrative pronoun
You → ✅ Personal pronoun
Who → Interrogative pronoun

questions.question: The roads of Dhaka are wider than ----- Rajbari.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
এখানে তুলনা করা হচ্ছে Dhaka-এর roads এবং Rajbari-এর roads এর মধ্যে।
যেহেতু roads plural, তাই তার পরিবর্তে plural demonstrative pronoun those ব্যবহার করতে হবে।
that of → singular (ভুল, কারণ roads plural)
those of → ✅ plural (সঠিক)
this of → ভুল
are → ব্যাকরণগতভাবে সঠিক নয়

questions.question: Every opposition candidate 'except she was' defeated in the election.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Every → singular subject
তাই verb হবে was (singular verb)
Except এর পরে objective case pronoun ব্যবহৃত হয় → her (not she)
❌ except she was → pronoun ও verb দুটোই ভুল
❌ except her were → verb ভুল (were plural)
❌ excepting she was → pronoun ও verb ভুল
✅ except her was → সঠিক গঠন

questions.question: The specialist ----- you want to meet is available only on Thursday.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
এখানে clauseটি হলো:
you want to meet (___)
এখানে you = subject
want = verb
to meet (___) → এখানে যে pronoun বসবে, তা verb “meet”-এর object হবে।
Object position-এ relative pronoun হলে whom ব্যবহার করা হয়।
whose → possession বোঝায় ❌
who → subject হিসেবে ব্যবহৃত হয় ❌
whom → object হিসেবে ব্যবহৃত হয় ✅
which → জিনিসের জন্য ব্যবহৃত হয় ❌

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: Everyone of the boy love to ride
Everyone of the boys loves to ride
Everyone of the boys love to ride
Everyone of the boy loves to ride
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Everyone → singular pronoun
তাই verb হবে loves (singular verb)
Everyone of the + plural noun → boys (plural হবে)
❌ Everyone of the boy love → noun ও verb দুটোই ভুল
❌ Everyone of the boys love → verb ভুল (love plural)
❌ Everyone of the boy loves → noun ভুল (boy singular)
✅ Everyone of the boys loves → সঠিক

questions.question: Any of you may take it. I don't care -----.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
এখানে “I don't care ___” clause-এর মধ্যে subject বা object বোঝাতে relative/interrogative pronoun লাগবে।
Who → কাউকে নির্দেশ করে (subject বা object হিসেবে casual use, এখানে object)
Which → জিনিসের জন্য ❌
What → “কি” বোঝায়, ব্যাকরণগতভাবে ঠিক নয় ❌
Whom → strictly object, কিন্তু modern casual English-এ “who” বেশি ব্যবহৃত হয় এবং এখানে ঠিক বসে ✅

questions.question: I want a red shirt. But they only had -----.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
“one” এখানে shirt-এর পরিবর্তে ব্যবহৃত হচ্ছে → singular pronoun referring back to “shirt”
Color + one pattern → correct usage: an orange one
a one orange → ভুল word order
one orange → color-এর আগে article “an” লাগে
an orange → “orange” singular noun হিসেবে লাগবে, কিন্তু এখানে shirt বোঝানো হচ্ছে

questions.question: The party was a disaster. There ----- there.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
এখানে মূল অর্থ: “party-এর মধ্যে কেউই ছিল না”
Negative meaning প্রকাশ করতে হবে → nobody
Verb agreement: singular → was
❌ wasn't nobody → double negative (ভুল)
❌ was anybody → positive sense, কিন্তু sentence negative context
❌ was somebody → positive sense

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: I shall be glad to help everyone of my boys in their studies
I shall be glad to help everyone of my boy in his studies
I shall be glad to help everyone of my boys in his studies
I shall be glad to help everyone of my boy in studies
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Everyone → singular pronoun, তাই his ব্যবহার হবে, না যে plural pronoun their।
Boys → plural noun after “everyone of my …”
Verb/Pronoun agreement:
❌ Option A → their (plural pronoun) ভুল
❌ Option B → boy (singular noun, but context says multiple boys)
❌ Option D → boy singular & “in studies” incomplete

questions.question: Either of these ----- to the airport.[]
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation of options:
A. road lead → singular noun + plural verb ❌
B. roads leads → plural noun + singular verb ❌ (subject is “Either”, not “roads”)
C. roads lead → plural noun + plural verb ❌
D. road leads → singular noun + singular verb ❌ (doesn’t match “these”)

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: Neither of the two player was successful
Neither of the two players were successful
Neither of the two players was successful
Neither of the two player were successful
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Neither → always singular, so verb must be was (singular)
of the two players → prepositional phrase, doesn’t change verb number
Common mistakes in options:
❌ A → “player” singular, but should match plural “two players” in the phrase
❌ B → “were” → plural verb ❌
❌ D → “player” + “were” → both wrong

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
questions.explanation:
A. I wish I were them! → “them” plural → wrong if referring to one person
B. I wish I were he! → grammatically correct in formal English ✅
C. I wish I were his! → ❌ “his” = possessive
D. I wish I were him! → ✅ natural, correct in spoken & written modern English

questions.question: Whoever' is a ---[]
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
Whoever = compound relative pronoun
It is formed by combining who + ever and is used to introduce a subordinate clause.
Examples:
Whoever comes first will get a prize.
You may choose whoever you like.
Other options:
Demonstrative pronoun → this, that, these, those ❌
Distributive pronoun → each, every, either, neither ❌
Personal pronoun → I, you, he, she, we, they ❌

questions.question: Nobel prize is considered the highest honour ----- can be achieved in certain fields of work.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Here, “that” introduces a relative clause describing “the highest honour.”
Sentence structure:
the highest honour (that) can be achieved → relative clause correctly modifies “honour.”
Other options:
which → could also work, but in restrictive clauses “that” is preferred ✅
it → wrong, doesn’t fit grammatically ❌
none of the above → ❌

questions.question:
I gave him all the money
 ----- I had.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
That → relative pronoun used to introduce a restrictive relative clause describing “all the money.”
Sentence structure:
all the money (that) I had → specifies which money
Other options:
which → could work, but “that” is preferred in restrictive clauses ✅
what → ❌ doesn’t fit after “all the money”
those → ❌ refers to plural objects, not appropriate here

questions.question: It should be ----- []
options: her with whom you share your ideas, not me
her with whom you share your ideas, not I
she with whom you share your ideas, not me
she with whom you share your ideas, not I
questions.explanation:
A → her … me ❌ first pronoun wrong
B → her … I ❌ first pronoun wrong, second pronoun wrong
C → she … me ✅ This is correct
D → she … I ❌ second pronoun wrong

questions.question: Which of the following has an emphatic use of the reflexive pronoun ?[]
options: She saw herself in the mirror
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
Reflexive pronouns can be used in two main ways:
Normal reflexive → when the subject and object are the same:
She saw herself in the mirror → “herself” refers back to “she”
Emphatic (intensive) use → to emphasize the subject:
I myself did the job → “myself” emphasizes I
Analyze options:
A → normal reflexive ❌
B → intensive reflexive “himself” ✅ (emphasizing “he”), but less direct than C
C → ✅ emphatic use (strong emphasis on “I”)
D → normal reflexive / emphasis depending on context, but standard usage is normal

questions.question: Please vote for the member ----- has done the most for our village.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The clause “who you believe has done the most” is a relative clause modifying “member.”
Who → relative pronoun referring to member (person)
Verb tense in main clause: you believe (present tense) → matches naturally
Other options:
whom you believe → technically could be object, but here “member” is subject of “has done,” so who is correct ❌
who you believed → past tense ❌ (changes meaning)
that you believe → grammatically possible, but for people “who” is preferred ✅

questions.question: Correct the sentence : 'Whoever objects to me' going to the convention ought to state his position promptly.[]
questions.explanation:
“Whoever” → subject of “objects”
“to me” → object of preposition to
“going to the convention” → participial phrase modifying “whoever”

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: It is I who am responsible for this
It is me who am responsible for this
It is me whom is responsible for this
It is that is responsible for this
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
After “It is …”, the pronoun should be in the subjective case → I (not me).
Relative clause: who am responsible → “who” refers to “I” (singular), so the verb am agrees with “I.”
Other options:
B → “me who am …” ❌ object pronoun after “It is” is incorrect
C → “me whom is …” ❌ both pronoun and verb are wrong
D → “It is that is responsible” ❌ awkward and incorrect

questions.question: The best of the correct sentences is ---[]
options: I hope you will excuse my leaving early
I hope you will excuse me leaving early
I hope you will excuse me for my leaving early
I hope you will excuse of my  leaving early
questions.explanation:
The word “excuse” is followed by a noun or a gerund (verb + -ing acting as a noun), not by a personal pronoun with a gerund.
Correct: excuse my leaving early → “my leaving” is a gerund phrase, properly acting as the object of “excuse.”
Incorrect: excuse me leaving early → sounds informal and less grammatically precise.
Option C (excuse me for my leaving early) is wordy and redundant. English prefers the simpler my leaving directly.
Option D (excuse of my leaving early) is incorrect because “excuse of” is never used; “excuse” doesn’t take the preposition “of.”

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: Neither of them saw each other
Neither of them saw the other
Neither of them saw one another
questions.explanation:
“Neither” refers to one of the two, so when talking about two people, the correct reference is “the other”, not “each other” or “one another.”
Each other / One another → usually used for reciprocal actions involving more than two (for one another, sometimes for two as well, but “the other” is more precise with “neither”).
Option A (Neither of them saw each other) is incorrect because “each other” is not the preferred choice with “neither.”
Option C (Neither of them saw one another) is awkward; “one another” is generally for more than two people, though some might accept it.

questions.question: Mark the correct sentence[]
options: One of the boys lost one's pen
One of the boys' lost one's pen
One of the boys lost his pen
One of the boy's lost his pen
questions.explanation:
“One of the boys” means a single boy from a group, so the pronoun referring back to “one” should be singular: “his”.
✅ Correct: One of the boys lost his pen
Option A (lost one's pen) is wrong because “one's” is a general, impersonal pronoun. Here, we are talking about a specific boy, not a generic “one.”
Option B (boys' lost one's pen) is wrong because the apostrophe after boys would incorrectly make it plural possessive, which doesn’t fit the meaning.
Option D (one of the boy's lost his pen) is wrong because boy's (singular possessive) cannot represent a group. We need boys (plural) to indicate the group.

questions.question: It was so dark that the security guard could not see ---[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is negative in meaning: “could not see…”. After a negative idea, English uses “anyone” rather than “somebody” or “nobody.”
✅ Correct: It was so dark that the security guard could not see anyone.
Option A (nobody) could also make sense informally: “could not see nobody”—but in standard English, double negatives like that are grammatically wrong.
Option B (somebody) is wrong, because “somebody” is used in positive statements, not negative ones.
Option D (none) doesn’t fit grammatically here. “None” is usually used without a following object: e.g., None of the guards were able to see.

questions.question: That young man to ----- we owe many thanks saved our mother's life after the car accident.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is talking about “that young man” as the object of the verb in the relative clause: “…we owe many thanks [to him]…”.
In formal English, the relative pronoun “whom” is used for the object of a verb or preposition.
Option C (who) is used for the subject of a clause, not the object. Here, the young man is the object of “owe”, so “who” is incorrect.
Option B (which) is for things, not people.
Option D (whose) shows possession, which doesn’t fit here.
✅ Correct sentence:
That young man, whom we owe many thanks, saved our mother’s life after the car accident.

questions.question: We cannot believe that the man 'whose' saved you from drowning.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is talking about “the man” as the subject of the relative clause: “…who saved you from drowning.”
When the person is the subject of the relative clause, we use who.
Option A (that) could work in informal English, but “who” is preferred for people.
Option B (whom) is used for the object of a verb or preposition, but here the man did the saving—he is the subject, so “whom” is wrong.
Option D (by whom) would be used only if the sentence were in the passive voice: “…the man by whom you were saved…”
✅ Correct sentence:
We cannot believe that the man who saved you from drowning.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: The announcer awarded the prize to Jamil and myself
The announcer awarded the prize to Jamil and me
The announcer awarded the prize to Jamil and I
The announcer awarded the prize to I and Jamil
questions.explanation:
The preposition “to” requires an object pronoun, not a subject pronoun.
Object pronouns: me, him, her, us, them
Subject pronouns: I, he, she, we, they
Option A (Jamil and myself) is incorrect because “myself” is a reflexive pronoun, which can only be used to refer back to the subject:
✅ Correct: I awarded the prize to myself
❌ Incorrect: awarded the prize to myself when the subject is someone else
Option C (Jamil and I) and D (I and Jamil) are wrong because “I” is a subject pronoun, not the object of “to.”

questions.question: When a man tended to know how I had got ----- contact number, I told him that I was given it by a relative of -----[]
questions.explanation:
Possessive pronouns are used when something belongs to someone. In this sentence, the contact number belongs to a relative of the man, so we need “his”:
✅ Correct: …I was given it by a relative of his.
Breaking the sentence down:
“…a relative of his” = a relative belonging to him
Using him instead of his here would be grammatically wrong.
Option A (him/him), B (his/him), C (him/his) are all wrong because the first or second pronoun must be possessive.

questions.question: John's car runs better than -----.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is comparative: John's car runs better than ___.
The comparison is about the car, not the person.
So we need the possessive form to compare John’s car vs Mary’s car.
Option breakdown:
A (Mary’s brother) → wrong, we’re not comparing a brother, but the car.
B (Mary) → wrong, would imply comparing a car to a person.
C (Mary’s) → correct, shorthand for Mary’s car.
D (her brother) → wrong for the same reason as A.

questions.question: A baby learns the meaning of words as ----- are spoken by others and later uses ----- in sentences.[]
questions.explanation:
First blank: “A baby learns the meaning of words as ___ are spoken by others…”
The subject is words, which is plural, so we use they.
✅ Correct: words as they are spoken by others
Second blank: “…and later uses ___ in sentences.”
The baby uses the words, so the object pronoun them is correct.
✅ Correct: uses them in sentences
Option A (their, they) → wrong, “their” is possessive, but we need a subject pronoun first.
Option C (they, themselves) → wrong, “themselves” is reflexive and not needed here.
Option D (it, them) → wrong, “words” is plural, so “it” is incorrect.

questions.question: One should respect ----- parents.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is a general statement: “One should respect parents.”
When making general statements with “one”, the corresponding possessive pronoun is “one’s”.
Option breakdown:
A (his) → could work in traditional usage, but modern English prefers one’s for general statements.
B (their) → incorrect, “their” is plural and doesn’t match the singular “one.”
C (one’s) → correct.
D (ones) → incorrect, “ones” is plural, not possessive.

questions.question: Find the correct sentence[]
options: It is none of your business
It is no one your business
It is not one your business
It is not any your business
questions.explanation:
A(It is none of your business) → correct.
B (It is no one your business) → wrong, “no one” refers to people, not things, and the syntax is incorrect.
C (It is not one your business) → wrong, not idiomatic.
D (It is not any your business) → incorrect syntax; “any” needs “of” (any of your business) but even then, it’s not standard.

questions.question: Which one is correct ?[]
options: The rice of Dinajpur is better than that of Dhaka
The rice of Dinajpur is better than Dhaka
The rice of Dinajpur are better than Dhaka
Dinajpur's rice is better than Dhaka
questions.explanation:
A (The rice of Dinajpur is better than that of Dhaka) → correct.
B (…better than Dhaka) → wrong, it incorrectly compares rice to a city.
C (The rice of Dinajpur are…) → wrong, “rice” is uncountable, so we use is, not are.
D (Dinajpur’s rice is better than Dhaka) → same mistake as B; comparing rice to a city.

questions.question: The country is about to go bilingual , with two official languages, but ----- of them is English.[]
questions.explanation:
A  (Both) → would mean both are English, which is opposite of the meaning.
B (None) → usually for more than two things, though sometimes acceptable for two.
C (No) → grammatically incomplete here.
D (Neither) → correct, properly refers to not one of the two languages.

questions.question: Rahim found a laptop in the classroom, but could not determine ------- it belonged to.[]
questions.explanation:
A (whom) → used for the object of a verb or preposition, but here the person is the subject of “told,” so wrong.
B (who) → correct, subject of “told.”
C (whose) → shows possession, which is not needed here.
D (that) → can sometimes replace “who,” but who is preferred for people in formal English.

questions.question: They asked us, Hamid and ----- whether we thought that the statistics has been presented fairly and accurately.[]
questions.explanation:
A (I) → subject pronoun, incorrect here because it’s the object of “asked”.
B (me) → correct, object pronoun.
C (my) → possessive adjective, does not fit.
D (mine) → possessive pronoun, does not fit as an object here

questions.question: Tell me ----- told you about it.[]
questions.explanation:
A (whom) → used for the object of a verb or preposition, but here the person is the subject of “told,” so wrong.
B (who) → correct, subject of “told.”
C (whose) → shows possession, which is not needed here.
D (that) → can sometimes replace “who,” but “who” is the more precise choice for a person.

questions.question: Identify the correct syntax.[]
questions.explanation:
A (You, he and I) → correct, follows the proper order.
B (He, you and I) → wrong order; third person comes first instead of second.
C (I, you and he) → wrong order; first person comes first, which is less formal and generally avoided.
D (None) → incorrect because A is correct.

questions.question: I asked you ------- of these shoes you think would go with my outfit.[]
questions.explanation:
A(whose) → shows possession, but this sentence is not about ownership.
B (who) → refers to people, not things like shoes.
C (which) → correct, used for selecting items from a set.
D (that) → could work in defining clauses, but after “asked you ___ of these shoes,” the grammatically correct and natural choice is which.

questions.question: I didn't buy ----- in the end.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is negative: “I didn’t buy ___ in the end.”
After a negative verb like didn’t, English uses any-words (anything, anyone, anywhere) instead of some-words.
Option breakdown:
A (nothing) → double negative if used with “didn’t”: I didn’t buy nothing ❌ (informal or nonstandard)
B (something) → usually used in positive statements, not after a negative verb.
C (everybody) → refers to people, not things you can buy.
D (anything) → correct for negative statements about things.

questions.question: A laptop of ----- has been lost[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is: “A laptop of ___ has been lost.”
We are referring to ownership. The correct possessive pronoun to replace “my laptop” is mine.
Option breakdown:
A (my) → possessive adjective, must be followed by a noun (e.g., my laptop), so it doesn’t fit after “of.”
B (mine) → correct; it stands alone as the object of “of.”
C (me) → object pronoun, doesn’t show possession.
D (I) → subject pronoun, not possessive, so wrong.

questions.question: I couldn't buy anything because ----- of the shop was open.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is: “I couldn’t buy anything because ___ of the shop was open.”
We are talking about not a single one of the shops being open, so the correct pronoun is none (meaning “not one”).
Option breakdown:
A (all) → would mean everything was open, which is the opposite of the meaning.
B (no one) → refers to people, but the subject here is shops, so wrong.
C (none) → correct, refers to things (shops) and matches the negative meaning.
D (nothing) → grammatically wrong here; “nothing of the shop” doesn’t fit.

questions.question: She was so fastidious that ----- of the three houses were to her liking.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is: “She was so fastidious that ___ of the three houses were to her liking.”
None means not one of them, which fits the meaning of the sentence: she didn’t like any of the houses.
Option breakdown:
A (neither) → only works for two items, but here there are three houses, so incorrect.
B (either) → refers to one of two items, so wrong.
C (none) → correct for three or more items.
D (no one) → refers to people, not things like houses, so wrong.

questions.question: The red coat belonged to him but the brown one was -----.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is: “The red coat belonged to him but the brown one was ___.”
We are referring to ownership. The proper possessive pronoun for “I” is mine.
✅ Correct: the brown one was mine
Option breakdown:
A (my) → possessive adjective, must be followed by a noun (e.g., my coat), so wrong here.
B (me) → object pronoun, doesn’t show ownership, so wrong.
C (mine) → correct, replaces the noun phrase and shows possession.
D (mines) → incorrect; “mines” is plural or a noun unrelated to pronouns.

questions.question: Manzur with ------- I work, helped him.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is: “Manzur, with ___ I work, helped him.”
The relative pronoun refers to Manzur, the object of the preposition “with”.
When the person is the object of a preposition, we use whom.
Option breakdown:
A (who) → used for subjects, but here Manzur is the object of “with,” so wrong.
B (which) → used for things, not people.
C (that) → can sometimes replace “who/whom,” but after a preposition like “with,” standard grammar prefers whom.
D (whom) → correct.
